judge_assessment.explanation: The numbers the judge verified are all correct -- 12 sin35 = 6.8829 -> 6.88; 14 tan52 = 17.9192 -> 17.92; atan(7/24) = 16.2602 -> 16.26; 20 cos41 = 15.0942 -> 15.09; 40 tan38 = 31.2514 -> 31.25; 10 sin30 = 5 -- and so are all six declared traps, including the two radian-mode ones I recomputed independently (14 tan(52 rad) = -84.75 and 40 tan(38 rad) = 12.41). Where I part company is the judge's 'manual_items_reviewed: 0' being treated as unremarkable on a sheet whose entire format is diagnosis. verify.json declares no manual items at all, yet the worksheet requires a written diagnosis in four places: problem 2 'Say what it is, then give the correct value of x'; problem 3 'Name the error, then give <A correctly'; problem 5 'Find what his calculator is doing and give the correct height'; problem 6(b) 'Which side of this triangle is 8.66, and which ratio did Sasha use to get it? Answer in one sentence beside your work'; and problem 1 also asks 'Write the ratio you chose before you compute'. The answer key itself treats 6(b) as a graded written answer -- 'Grading note: accept "the longer leg, opposite the 60 degree angle, found with sin 60 (or cos 30)" as a full-credit answer to part (b)' -- and final_response.md then tells the teacher the opposite: 'All 6 worksheet answers ... are machine-verified with SymPy ... and no manual items, so the build finished all-green (exit 0) rather than with manual-review flags'. The prompt for this case explicitly required 'clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review', so this is an instruction-following miss the 32/32 does not reflect.

strengths_to_preserve: The three error types are cleanly separated and each planted number is reproducible from the wrong method: radian mode twice (-84.75 from tan(52 rad) and 12.41 from tan(38 rad)), an inverted inverse once (atan(24/7) = 73.74), and wrong-ratio choices (12 cos35 = 9.83, 20 sin41 = 13.12, 10 sin60 = 8.66). Each trap expression in verify.json computes exactly the number printed in the worksheet.

Problem 5 teaches the sanity check before the fix: the worksheet itself argues 'That height is less than half the distance he is standing away, even though the angle is close to 45 degrees -- so the number cannot be right', so the student diagnoses from a size argument rather than by re-keying the calculation.

Problem 6(b) uses a wrong answer that is a REAL length of the same triangle -- 8.66 is 5 sqrt(3), the other leg -- so the error cannot be caught by a plausibility check, only by naming the angle you are working from; the key says exactly that.

The key's closing asymmetry is the most useful sentence in the packet and is carried into the study guide's watch-out box: 'a mode error usually produces an absurd number, a wrong ratio produces a believable one', which is why problem 1's key notes that cosine's 9.83 also passes the leg-shorter-than-hypotenuse test.

root_causes.description: On a misconception-analysis sheet the graded response is the DIAGNOSIS, but the verification contract records only the repaired number. Because each problem carries a numeric entry, per-id coverage is satisfied and the written half disappears; the build then reports exit 0 with no manual flags, and the delivery message states as fact that nothing needs human review.
evidence: verify.json contains six entries (approx x4, triangle x2) and zero entries of type 'manual'.

worksheet.pdf problem 2: 'Her setup is right, so the fault is in the calculator. Say what it is, then give the correct value of x.'; problem 3: 'His arithmetic is fine; the ratio inside the inverse is not. Name the error, then give <A correctly.'; problem 5: 'Find what his calculator is doing and give the correct height of the pole'; problem 6(b): 'Which side of this triangle is 8.66, and which ratio did Sasha use to get it? Answer in one sentence beside your work.'

answer_key.pdf problem 6 ends with 'Grading note: accept "the longer leg, opposite the 60 degree angle, found with sin 60 (or cos 30)" as a full-credit answer to part (b)' -- a human grading instruction for an item declared machine-only.

final_response.md: 'All 6 worksheet answers and all 6 study-guide answers are machine-verified with SymPy -- four approx trigonometric computations, two triangle solves from raw givens, and no manual items, so the build finished all-green (exit 0) rather than with manual-review flags.'
machine_observation records gate_chain_manual_flags: false, so nothing downstream signals that four written diagnoses are ungraded.

improvements.title: Declare the written diagnosis in problems 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6(b) as manual instead of shipping the sheet as fully machine-verified
improvements.proposed_change: Add a gate that scans each \problem body for diagnosis cues ('say what it is', 'name the error', 'which ratio did', 'explain', 'find what ... is doing', 'answer in one sentence', 'write the ratio you chose') and fails the build unless that id carries a manual entry; and, because misconception-analysis is a declared instructional_mode in the task contract, have scripts/build.sh treat a worksheet in that mode with ZERO manual entries as a hard failure rather than an all-green exit 0. Add the same cross-check the key already implies: any 'Grading note' or manual-review bracket printed in answer_key.tex must correspond to a manual entry in verify.json.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: an error-analysis worksheet whose problem reads 'Name the error, then give <A correctly' with a verify.json holding a single approx entry and an answer key printing a 'Grading note' for that id. The gate must exit non-zero on both the cue rule and the key/verify cross-check, and must pass once a manual entry is added. curr-324 builds green today (exit 0, gate_chain_manual_flags false), so the test fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The teacher stops being told that a diagnosis-based sheet needs no human grading. Four written diagnoses -- the actual objective of the worksheet -- gain a desc stating what a correct answer must contain, and the delivery summary's claim matches the artifact.
improvements.risk: Cue matching can fire on narration inside a solution rather than a request in a problem, so it must read only \problem bodies; making zero-manual a hard failure for misconception mode could false-fail a legitimately all-numeric error-analysis sheet, so the rule should be overridable with an explicit author declaration.

case_summary: Mathematically exact and pedagogically sharp: six results (6.88, 17.92, 16.26, 15.09, 31.25, 5) and six traps (9.83, -84.75, 73.74, 13.12, 12.41, 8.66) all recompute correctly, the study guide's examples and try-its check out (13.79, 61.93, 23.55, and the -4.01 radian-mode demonstration), and the figures are generated from the same givens the verifier uses. The defect is in the verification contract, not the mathematics: this is an error-analysis sheet where four problems ask the student to name what went wrong -- and problem 6(b) even asks for 'one sentence' -- yet verify.json declares zero manual items, the build reports all-green exit 0, and final_response.md tells the teacher there are 'no manual items'. The answer key contradicts that by printing a grading note for 6(b). The judge recorded manual_items_reviewed: 0 and scored instruction_following 4, but the prompt explicitly asked that genuinely open responses be labelled for manual review.
